metric.why: Transformer and switchgear lead times stretched from months to years and now gate construction schedules as hard as permits do. Lead-time surveys are published by industry groups and research firms; watch the directory sources.
metric.definition: Order-to-delivery time for transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling plant, and high-end accelerators.

reading.body:
Equipment lead times, not construction permits or financing, now determine how fast data centers can be built for AI workloads.

Transformers, switchgear, generators, and cooling systems take years to deliver instead of months. This bottleneck sits downstream of the permit and funding decisions, which means projects can be approved and financed but cannot break ground on schedule. High-end accelerators face similar delays. The constraint is now physical: you cannot build a facility faster than suppliers can deliver the machines that convert power into computing capacity.

For AI specifically, this matters because scaling compute requires scaling power infrastructure in lockstep. A data center without transformers or switchgear cannot draw the grid power needed to run chips. Every month of delay in equipment delivery is a month the facility sits idle, unable to contribute compute to training or inference. This directly impacts the timeline from capital allocation to productive capacity.

The data does not cover whether lead times are lengthening, stabilizing, or improving, nor does it show which equipment categories are most constrained. It also does not quantify how much construction delay results from equipment wait times versus other factors. Lead times are an input to total project duration, not the output itself.
